title: The U.S.-China Summit: Too Big and Too Small to Fail
gist: CSIS's Scott Kennedy expects the September 2026 Trump-Xi summit to 'succeed' only because both leaders need calm (US midterms, wobbly bonds; Xi's 2027 Party Congress) and expectations are minimal: likely a roughly one-year extension of the trade ceasefire with more rare earth flows, small tariff cuts on $30B of goods and Boeing/ag deals, but no G2-style stewardship of global problems.

insights.claim: The US economy is strong mainly due to AI investment but has persistent inflation, rising unemployment and ballooning debt, with a wobbly bond market and rising yields signaling anxiety about foundational risks.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Rising yields and fiscal worries constrain Washington's appetite for trade escalation before midterms.
insights.quote: The bond market is already wobbly, with yields continuing to rise

insights.claim: With midterms approaching, the Trump administration has no interest in a crisis with China, while Xi, planning for the fall 2027 21st Party Congress that will likely grant him a fourth term, also benefits from stability amid shaky Chinese macro forecasts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Low near-term probability of a US-China trade shock through late 2027; supportive for China-exposed risk assets.
insights.locator: Beijing likely is computing a similar calculus

insights.claim: The US-China commercial ceasefire will likely be extended, with China allowing more rare earth exports to the US and others (Japan's access a US priority) and the US keeping cumulative tariffs on China no higher than at the October 2025 Busan meeting.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Eases rare earth supply risk for US and Japanese manufacturers; tariff ceiling reduces escalation tail.
insights.locator: Hence, observers can expect the current commercial ceasefire

insights.claim: Beijing wants the trade truce extended to the end of Trump's term while Washington prefers six months; the likely compromise is one more year.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Mark the ~one-year truce horizon (late 2027) as the next trade-risk window.
insights.quote: The obvious compromise would be one more year.
insights.locator: Beijing has reportedly sought to extend

insights.claim: Expected small deals include cutting tariffs to standard levels on $30 billion of each side's exports, more Boeing aircraft, aircraft component and agricultural purchases, an initial AI safety discussion, and softened language on Ukraine and the Persian Gulf.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Potential order headlines for Boeing and US farm exporters around the summit.
insights.locator: Too Small to Not Meet Expectations

insights.claim: Trump and Xi will likely meet again in November in Shenzhen and in December in Miami, producing more of the same incremental outcomes.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A cadence of leader meetings keeps US-China headline risk low through year-end.
insights.locator: Trump and Xi will likely meet in November

insights.claim: The US-China relationship is great power competition tempered by interdependence, a rough balance of power and domestic pressures—not a G2 co-stewardship of the international order.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Do not price structural US-China cooperation on macro imbalances, AI or climate; expect tactical truces only.
insights.quote: Although Trump and Xi will outwardly get along, this is not a G2.

insights.claim: The summit is a lost opportunity to address global macroeconomic imbalances, AI risks, the Ukraine and Middle East wars and climate change, pointing to a growing global leadership vacuum.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Leadership vacuum implies persistent geopolitical and imbalance risks without coordinated fixes.
insights.locator: Given the widening global distribution of power

insights.claim: The Trump administration pursues an 'imperial' foreign policy built on sovereignty, hard power and bilateralism, dismisses multilateral norms, climate and AI safety concerns, and suffers from a broken interagency process that leaves it bouncing between problems.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect ad hoc, transactional policymaking and elevated policy volatility.
insights.locator: But the Trump administration is inherently constrained

insights.claim: The uneasy trade truce with Beijing hinders US efforts to gain China's help on Ukraine and Iran, leaving Washington playing defense on multiple fronts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Linkage means trade calm may come at the expense of leverage on energy-relevant conflicts.
insights.locator: As a result, the administration’s strategy

insights.claim: Beijing is content to run out the clock on the Trump administration, keep EU pressure at bay and advance its own global governance via bodies like the SCO and the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO).
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: China-led parallel institutions, including in AI governance, will keep growing.
insights.locator: Conversely, Beijing could conceivably do much more
